trap.why: Write-back acknowledges before the data is durable, so a cache node failure loses writes, which is unacceptable for orders or money.
trap.probe: Durability trade-offs, and knowing the common default is cache-aside with delete-on-write.
trap.say: "Cache-aside with delete-on-write for most data; write-back only for loss-tolerant aggregates like view counts."

thesis: Write-through updates cache and store together, keeping them aligned at the cost of write latency. Write-back acknowledges after updating the cache and writes the store later: fast, but risks loss. Write-around writes only to the store and lets reads populate the cache, avoiding pollution with rarely read data. Most application caches use cache-aside with write-around plus invalidation.
pitch: The question is what happens on a write. Write-through: write to the store and the cache synchronously, so reads right after a write hit a fresh cache; writes are slower and you may cache data nobody reads. Write-back, or write-behind: write to the cache, acknowledge, and flush to the store asynchronously, which is great for write-heavy, loss-tolerant workloads like counters and metrics but dangerous for anything you can't lose, because a cache failure loses unflushed writes. Write-around: write only to the store, and the next read misses and loads it; best when written data is often not read soon, avoiding cache churn. In practice, for most services I'd use cache-aside: read from cache, on miss load from the database and populate; on write, update the database and delete the cache key, so the next read loads fresh data.

points.d: Synchronous write to store and cache. Reads after writes are fresh. Write latency includes both, and rarely read data still occupies cache.
Write to cache, acknowledge, persist later in batches. Lowest write latency and fewer store writes. Data loss if the cache fails before flushing; ordering and durability need care.
Write to the store only. The cache fills on read. Avoids polluting the cache with write-once data; first read after a write is a miss.
Application owns caching: read-through on miss, and on write update the database then delete (not update) the cache key.

points.h: Delete rather than update on write
points.d: Updating the cache on write can race with concurrent writes and leave a stale value. Deleting forces a fresh load; combined with TTLs, it bounds staleness.
Use write-back only when losing a window of writes is acceptable or the cache itself is durable and replicated.

decision: Cache-aside with delete-on-write for most application data. Write-through when reads immediately follow writes and a miss is expensive. Write-back for high-volume, loss-tolerant aggregates (view counts, rate counters). Write-around for write-heavy data that's rarely read back soon.
numbers: Write-back batching: 10,000 counter increments/s flushed every second as aggregated updates per key can turn into a few hundred database writes/s instead of 10,000.
pitfalls: Write-back for financial or order data, losing writes on a cache node failure.
Update-on-write races: two writers interleave and the cache ends up with the older value.
Write-through for data that's rarely read, filling the cache with cold entries.
Forgetting that the cache and the database can't be updated atomically; design for brief inconsistency.

followups.q: Why delete instead of update on write?
followups.a: With concurrent writers, 'update database then set cache' can apply in a different order to each store, leaving stale data. Delete makes the next read load whatever is current.

followups.q: Can delete-on-write still leave stale data?
followups.a: Yes, a reader can load an old value just before the write and put it into the cache just after the delete. TTLs bound the staleness; versioned keys or leases close the gap further.

followups.q: When would you use a read-through cache library?
followups.a: When you want the caching logic centralised (the cache loads from the store on miss), which simplifies application code but couples the cache to the data source.

example: A social app keeps post view counts with write-back: increments go to Redis and are flushed every 5 seconds, accepting the loss of a few seconds of counts on failure. Post content uses cache-aside: edits update Postgres and delete the cached post.
